journal_name: ACM Journal on Autonomous Transportation Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel game-theoretic decision-making paradigm for autonomous vehicles operating in complex urban environments where human-driven vehicles and pedestrians exhibit unpredictable behaviors. Unlike conventional rule-based or learning-based approaches that treat interaction as noise, we conceptualize the dynamic interaction between autonomous vehicles and heterogeneous road users as a hierarchical differential game. Our framework employs a hierarchical structure where strategic-level decisions (e.g., yielding, merging, overtaking) are modeled through Stackelberg game formulations, while tactical-level motions are governed by Nash equilibrium solutions in continuous action spaces. We prove existence and uniqueness conditions for the equilibrium states under mild regularity assumptions. Extensive simulations across 10,000 scenarios demonstrate that the proposed paradigm achieves 47% reduction in conservative behaviors compared to rule-based methods and 31% improvement in social compliance compared to state-of-the-art reinforcement learning approaches. The theoretical contributions include a unified mathematical framework that bridges traditional traffic flow theory with modern game theory, fundamentally shifting how autonomous vehicles perceive and respond to social interactions in mixed traffic. This paradigm shift enables autonomous systems to reason about others' intentions and anticipate adversarial behaviors rather than merely reacting to observed states.

This paper presents an enhanced probabilistic sensor fusion framework that significantly improves state estimation accuracy for autonomous vehicles operating under adverse weather conditions. Building upon the extended Kalman filter paradigm, we develop a novel multi-hypothesis fusion architecture that explicitly models sensor degradation modes and adaptively weights heterogeneous sensing modalities based on real-time confidence assessment. The core theoretical contribution lies in deriving a closed-form solution for optimal fusion weights under non-Gaussian noise distributions, extending the classical Kalman framework to handle heavy-tailed measurement errors characteristic of LiDAR and camera sensors in fog or heavy rain. We formulate the confidence estimation problem as a learned Bayesian inference task, trained on a dataset of 500,000 annotated sensor readings across diverse weather conditions. Experimental evaluation on both simulation and real-world data demonstrates a 23% improvement in position estimation accuracy and a 41% reduction in state estimation latency compared to existing adaptive fusion methods. The proposed framework maintains robust performance even when individual sensor modalities experience complete signal loss, achieving graceful degradation essential for safety-critical autonomous driving applications.

This paper presents AutoNav, a groundbreaking end-to-end autonomous navigation system that unifies perception, prediction, and planning through a single neural architecture trained with self-supervised objectives. Unlike traditional modular pipelines where each component is independently designed and optimized, AutoNav leverages a transformer-based architecture with cross-modal attention mechanisms that jointly process raw sensor streams (LiDAR point clouds, camera images, radar returns) and generate motion plans directly in the action space. The system introduces a novel temporal consistency module that enforces physical constraints across planning horizons, ensuring dynamic feasibility and collision avoidance without explicit post-processing. Key architectural innovations include a hierarchical tokenization scheme that abstracts semantic, geometric, and temporal features, and a differentiable trajectory optimization layer that enables gradient-based refinement of neural outputs. Extensive evaluation on benchmark datasets comprising 2 million real-world driving scenarios demonstrates superior performance in long-tail edge cases, with 34% fewer interventions required compared to industry-grade systems. AutoNav represents a paradigm shift toward unified neural autonomous systems that learn coordinated behaviors end-to-end rather than assembling independently validated modules.

This paper introduces V2X-Track, an enhanced vehicle-to-everything communication system for real-time cooperative perception in autonomous transportation networks. V2X-Track addresses critical latency and reliability challenges in V2X-assisted perception through three key architectural innovations: (1) a priority-aware message scheduling algorithm that dynamically allocates communication resources based on objects' relevance scores computed from trajectory prediction confidence; (2) an early fusion module that integrates V2X messages with on-board sensor data before object detection, enabling collaborative perception of occluded objects; and (3) a robust synchronization mechanism that compensates for communication delays and clock drift across heterogeneous vehicles and infrastructure nodes. The system is implemented as a distributed software architecture compatible with IEEE 802.11p and 5G cellular networks. Field tests conducted with 12 connected vehicles across urban and highway scenarios demonstrate 28% improvement in detection range for critical objects and 45% reduction in perception latency for V2X-equipped vehicles. Importantly, V2X-Track achieves these improvements while maintaining message delivery reliability above 99.5% under varying network congestion conditions, making it suitable for safety-critical cooperative driving applications.
